title: TB5-00177

Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXXXXX a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXX a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find her a Convention refugee, or, in the alternative, refer her claim back to the RPD for re-determination.
Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal. Background

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she is a Falun Gong practitioner. She alleges that after telling a friend that she was experiencing stress from her schooling, the friend recommended that she practice Falun Gong. She began practicing with the friend and joined her practice group as well. The group practice was subsequently raided and she went into hiding at the home of another friend. The Appellant recognized it was unsafe to remain in China and sought the assistance of a smuggler to leave the country. She travelled to the United States en route to Canada. While attempting to enter Canada illegally, she was apprehended by Canadian officials. The Appellant claims authorities in China are seeking to arrest her for her practice of Falun Gong. This led to her making a refugee claim in Canada.

The Appellant's claim for refugee protection was heard on November 3, 2014. In a decision on December 19, 2014, the RPD rejected the claim finding that the Appellant was not a credible witness and she was not a Falun Gong practitioner.

The Appellant submits that the RPD's determination is based on erroneous findings and as such, is unsustainable. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its credibility findings on the following three issues: a) Her ability to leave China using her own passport b) An unreasonable assessment of her supporting documents and c) An unreasonable assessment of the Appellant's sur place claim.

Counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the most recent Federal Court decision in Huruglica1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.2 [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."3

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL The RPD's findings

The RPD in its Reasons found: i. The claimant did not provide credible and trustworthy evidence of practicing Falun Gong in China. ii. The claimant was not wanted by the authorities in China for the practice of Falun Gong. iii. The claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in Canada and came to Canada in order to advance a fraudulent refugee claim. iv. There is insufficient evidence that the claimant's actions in Canada have come to the attention of Chinese authorities.

A review of the Appellant's Memorandum4 by the RAD notes the Appellant does not dispute the findings of the RPD in respect of the claimant's Falun Gong practice in China. The RPD misapprehended the evidence regarding the applicant's ability to leave China undetected using her own passport

The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the Appellant's ability to leave China using her own passport. The RPD noted that despite documentary evidence that security services are successful in preventing persons who are wanted from leaving the country and considering that her passport was issued after she was already wanted by the PSB due to her involvement in Falun Gong, the Appellant was still able to leave China. The RPD concluded that the use of a smuggler without details of how a smuggler was able to circumvent the vast security capabilities, was insufficient to explain the claimant's ability to secure a passport and leave without a problem.
The Appellant submits that the evidence before the RPD makes it clear that there is no certainty with respect to whether the database exists.

The Appellant relies on item 10.3 listed in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for China that states: "it was not until February 11, 2009 that the Chinese Ministry of Public Security even selected a technology company - China Information Security Technology - to deliver the system." 5

Although the Appellant alleges the RPD misapprehended the evidence, the RAD finds that it is the Appellant who has misapprehended the evidence she relies on. A careful reading of the document relied upon reveals that the document does not state that the PSB selected the technology company on February 11, 2009. Rather, the document refers to an article dated February 11, 2009 in which it is stated that a technology company was selected, but it does not provide a date of when that selection was made. The article is as follows: An 11 February 2009 Datamonitor article indicates that the Ministry of Public Security chose China Information Security Technology (CIST) to deliver police-use geographic information systems (PGIS) nationally. PGIS is said to offer increased coordination and monitoring amongst the mobile police workforce, allowing the command centre to see and communicate with ground-level police (Datamonitor 11 Feb. 2009).6 (bold emphasis added)

The Appellant also quotes the same document as stating that the "a number of provincial level cities and municipalities would have standardized and integrated elements of this technology system in three years, after which these systems will be implemented nationwide."7

The RAD finds that the Appellant has taken this statement out of context. The Appellant fails to acknowledge that the paragraph quoted is referring to the second phase of the implementation of the system. The Appellant also fails to acknowledge that the article providing this information was dated in 2009; however, there is no indication in the article when the system was implemented.

The article states that: ...this national PGIS initiative is part of phase two of the Golden Shield project and aims to "establish an integrated platform connecting all variations of PGIS systems throughout the country" in order to share information across various public service departments and police divisions (Ibid.). It is estimated that 100 provincial-level cities and municipalities will have standardized and integrated PGIS systems in three years, after which these systems will be implemented nationwide (Ibid.).8
In fact, the same document relied upon by the Appellant provides evidence that the Golden Shield project was operational as early as 2003.

The Appellant also refers to Wei9 to support her argument. In that case, the reviewing court took exception to the panel's reliance on the documentary evidence related to the Golden Shield project. In particular, the court stated: "The information does not confirm that a centralised information sharing system was in place; rather it discusses the intention to put such a network in place."10
However, the RAD notes that the decision in Wei11 was based on the documentary evidence that existed in 2010. In the case at hand, the RPD relies on the documentary evidence in the record today.
Again, the RAD notes that the same National Documentation Package relied upon by the Appellant also states with certainty that the Golden Shield project is operational.

A researcher, who has conducted research and published on the Chinese policing system for fifteen years and who was previously a professor of Chinese and East Asian Politics at Western Michigan University, stated the following in correspondence with the Research Directorate:12 China's Public Security Departments absolutely do have nationwide computer information sharing networks, and have been working hard to develop and expand those for at least a decade.... [A] fair amount is published about them in Chinese language police journals. One does read complaints about provincial police departments not being willing to share information with each other, however. For Chinese readers, a good deal of information about nationwide arrest warrants is openly available on the webpage of the Ministry of Public Security (www.mps.gov.cn) and on the webpages of the various provincial public security departments. There has really been an explosion of this online police information in the past 6-7 years. (11 May 2009).

The RAD also notes that the United Kingdom Operational Guidance Note, dated 29 August 2012, states the following: The Chinese police have access to a National Computer Database, known as Golden Shield Project. Its aim is to improve policing, and there are strict regulations on the use of the database. It holds information on population information, criminal records information, information on criminal fugitives, information on stolen vehicles, information on passports and exit/entry data, information on registered cars and drivers, information on police officers and information on key fire-prevention units. All police departments at county level and above (i.e. police departments at provincial, city and county levels) and most grass-roots units (police units below county level) can now connect to this system. There are some small police departments in remote areas that cannot yet connect to Golden Shield.13
Based on the foregoing, it is clear that such a system is in place.

Further to this the RAD notes the Appellant does not address the issue raised by the RPD in respect of the plausibility of a genuine Chinese passport being issued to her following the time she alleges the PSB began to search for her on xxx, 2014.14 In reviewing the audio recording of the hearing the RAD finds the Appellant was questioned as to how she obtained the passport. Her response was, "It was arranged by the snakehead". The Appellant was further asked how this was arranged and she answered, "I'm not sure". The RPD concluded, having considered both the documentary evidence as well as the Appellant's testimony, the mere use of a smuggler without any details of how the smuggler acted to circumvent the vast security network is insufficient to explain the Appellant's ability to obtain a passport and leave China safely if the authorities were seeking her.

The RAD in addition reviewed the documentary evidence in respect of the issuing of Chinese Biometric Passports which states:15 ...the conditions, time limit, and charge for applying for the ordinary e-passport are [the] same as those of the past [but in the course of applying] the procedures of collecting the applicant's finger prints and the applicant signing [his or her] name on site are added.

The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would provide some supporting testimony to confirm that in the very least she supplied these items to the smuggler to obtain the passport. When one further considers that the documentary evidence16 states that passports are issued by the entry-exit control department of the public security organ under the people's government at or above the county level where his residence is registered.

The RAD having assessed and considered the evidence in this issue, finds this information buttresses the RPD conclusion that the Appellant would be unable to obtain a passport and leave China while being sought by the authorities.

The Federal Court has stated: The RPD is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality, and it may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.17 Where the RPD finds a lack of credibility based on inferences concerning the plausibility of evidence, there must be a basis in the evidence to support such inferences.18
In this case, there is an evidential foundation for the RPD's findings. In having independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD finds that it supports the RPD's finding on this issue.

The RAD also notes that the Appellant has not tendered any persuasive evidence that the PSB or any other authority in China is pursuing her. On the basis of the totality of the RPD's findings affirmed in these reasons, the assessment by the RAD and the lack of persuasive evidence to the contrary; the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegations that she was a Falun Gong practitioner in China, that her Falun Gong group was raided and that she is being pursued by the PSB is not credible. The RPD engaged in unreasonable analysis with respect to the Appellant's supporting documents

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it misconstrued the evidence in its assessment of a letter submitted in support of her practice of Falun Gong in Canada. The Appellant alleges the RPD dismissed the document partially on the basis that the Appellant's sister did not testify in support of her claim. The Appellant argues that the panel came to the conclusion that the letter was not a reflection of the Appellant's Falun Gong practice in Canada because the author of the letter was a fellow refugee claimant.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard. The RAD in reviewing the record, finds that the Appellant's argument in respect of the RPD having rejected the letter based on the claimant's sister not testifying in support of her claim is taken out of context.

The RPD roots its findings in a number of credibility concerns outlined in its reasons. The RPD went into extensive detail in describing credibility findings in respect of the Appellant's sister - a previous refugee claimant whose claim was allegedly also submitted on the basis of having been a Falun Gong practitioner. The RPD found further contradiction in the Appellant's actions of utilizing a stranger whom she testified that she knows little about to attest to her identity as a Falun Gong practitioner in the form of a letter rather than her sister.

The RAD in reviewing the audio recording of the hearing noted that the Appellant's testimony in reference to the individual who authored the letter seemed vague and lacked specificity. The RAD further notes the record reflects the Appellant was questioned about the content of the letter. Her testimony in this regard was also hesitant, vague and lacking in specificity. The RAD finds the Appellant's ambiguous testimony further undermines the claimant's credibility as well as her identity as a Falun Gong practitioner and undermines the credibility of the document.

The RAD in evaluating the document19 notes the letter is dated October 4, 2014 and states that the author met the Appellant on September 13, 2014, indicating that the author of the document has known the Appellant for three weeks. Further to this the RAD finds the document indicates (as the Appellant confirmed in testimony) that the individuals perform the five exercises associated with Falun Gong together. The RAD notes that the letter may confirm the Appellant may have learned the exercises associated with the practice of Falun Gong. Master Li, the founder of Falun Gong in the text Zhuan Falun explains the performance of the exercises alone without regard for the philosophy of Falun Gong does not define that individual as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. In addition the author of the letter states, "Ms. xxxx is a true Falun Gong practitioner". The RAD finds there was no evidence adduced in the record to indicate that the author of this letter has the expertise to make such a judgment and as such, little weight can be afforded to his assessment of the genuineness of the Appellant's alleged practice.

Additionally the RAD has examined the "List of Falun Gong Co-practitioners"20 submitted in evidence at the RPD hearing. The RAD notes the document is dated July 11, 2014. Examination of the Basis of Claim (BOC) document21 confirms the Appellant did not enter Canada for the first time until August 30, 2014; well over one month after her alleged co-practitioners attested to her practice of Falun Gong. This significant contradiction in dates undermines the authenticity of the document and as such, the RAD assigns it little evidentiary weight. The RAD also notes that the author of the letter submitted in support of the Appellant's practice of Falun Gong appears on this document. Given that the author of the letter included his name on a document attesting to the fact that he was a co-practitioner of the Appellant at a time when the Appellant was not yet in Canada, the RAD finds that the credibility of the letter is also undermined.

The Appellant also submits that the RPD finding with regard to her practice of Falun Gong was speculative. The RAD finds that the Appellant's argument has some merit. The RAD's review of the RPD's decision finds its analysis is not well articulated and its statements are unclear, leading the RPD to draw what at best can be described as a speculative conclusion. The RAD finds that the RPD erroneously found that the letter of support was part of an organized effort to support the advancement of fraudulent refugee claims. The RAD finds there is no basis in the record for the RPD to come to this conclusion. It is unfortunate that the RPD has implied that there is an organized conspiracy to advance fraudulent claims however there remains sufficient reason to place little weight on the documents22 in question.

The RAD concludes after its own review and assessment of the evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, these documents are not genuine documents. The RAD finds that the submission of these non-genuine documents undermines the Appellant's credibility and further undermines the genuineness as a Falun Gong practitioner in China and in Canada. The RPD's analysis of the appellant's sur place claim was unreasonable

The Appellant submits that the RPD's sur place analysis is erroneous because it fails to explain why the applicant's Falun Gong practice group would not be watched by the Chinese authorities. The Appellant quotes the below-noted extract from the RPD's reasons: The panel has insufficient evidence to suggest the claimant's limited actions in Canada, likely done to advance her refugee claim, have come to the attention of Chinese authorities and so would cause her any problems upon her return.

The Appellant argues that, even if the Appellant was not a genuine practitioner of Falun Gong, she could still be at risk if her Falun Gong activities in Canada came to the attention of Chinese authorities. The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to consider whether there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution of the Appellant given her public practice of Falun Gong and the documented monitoring that takes place by the Chinese government.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard. The RAD finds that the RPD did consider the risk to the Appellant if the Chinese authorities became aware of her Falun Gong activities in Canada. Having found that the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China, the RPD considered whether the Appellant's activities in Canada would place her at risk of persecution. Having previously found the Appellant's testimony with regard to her Falun Gong affiliation in China not credible, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that her claim that she was a Falun Gong practitioner in China was made to further a fraudulent refugee claim. The RAD having conducted a full review and assessment of the record arrives at the same conclusion and supports the finding of the RPD.

The RAD also finds as noted by the RPD that there was no persuasive evidence adduced at the hearing or in her BoC form that the Appellant's practice of Falun Gong in Canada has come to the attention of Chinese authorities or that she would be perceived to be a genuine practitioner. In this respect, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court Trial Division decision in Wang,23 which held that a sur place claim could not be maintained in the absence of evidence that the making of the refugee claim had specifically come to the attention of the authorities of the claimant's country of origin. The Appellant does not submit that the RPD has misconstrued the facts in Wang.24

The RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that her desire to initiate the practice of Falun Gong took place as a result of circumstances which occurred in China. She alleges her continued practice of her alleged belief system in Canada is based on her adherence to her practice in China. Having found that she was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China and having no evidence of conversion in Canada, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of the findings noted above, that the Appellant joined a Falun Gong group in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.
In the context as noted above and on the basis of the totality of evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellant is not a genuine adherent of Falun Gong, nor would she be perceived to be one in China.

The Appellant has alleged that the RPD erred in rejecting her claim. Notwithstanding the error made by the RPD in drawing a speculative conclusion, the RAD finds after its review and assessment of all of the evidence in the record, that the cumulative adverse credibility findings and significant uncontested credibility findings of the RPD are sufficient for the RAD to confirm the RPD's overall determination.

The RAD finds that, on the basis of the totality of the evidence in this appeal, the Appellant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in China.

Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed. (signed) "Robert Bebbington" Robert Bebbington April 15, 2015 Date 1 Huruglica, Bujar v. M.C.I. (F.C. no.
